Proposition
[Riemann's characterization of constant sectional curvature]

Source: petersen:page-0101, petersen:page-0102, petersen:page-0103 ↗ def:pet-ch3-sectional-curvature ↗ def:pet-ch3-curvature-operator ↗ prop:pet-ch3-curvature-symmetries ↗ lem:pet-ch3-bivector-jacobi-identity

1. ch3:3.1.3The following are equivalent, for fixed $p\in M$ and $k\in \mathbb R$:

  1. $\sec (\pi )=k$ for all $2$-planes $\pi \subset T_pM$;

  2. $R(v_1,v_2)v_3=-k(v_1\wedge v_2)(v_3)$ for all $v_1,v_2,v_3\in T_pM$;

  3. $R_v(w)=k\cdot (w-g(w,v)v)=k\cdot \operatorname {prj}_{v^\perp }(w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$ and unit $v$;

  4. $\mathfrak R(\omega )=k\cdot \omega $ for all $\omega \in \Lambda ^2T_pM$.

Proof

↗ prop:pet-ch3-riemann-constant-curvature-equivalence

\sketch By subsection 1.3 and subsection 1.3, conditions (2) and (3) are equivalent by evaluating the bivector map on a unit vector, and either gives (1) after pairing with $w$. Conversely, compare $R$ with

\[ R_k(x,y)z=-k(x\wedge y)(z). \]

Their difference has the curvature symmetries; the first Bianchi identity for $R_k$ follows from subsection 1.2. It vanishes on every expression $D(v,w,w,v)$, so polarization and Bianchi force $D=0$, proving (2). The defining pairing of $\mathfrak R$ in subsection 1.2 then makes (2) equivalent to $\mathfrak R=k\, \mathrm{id}$, which is (4).

□
